summary: For ages 5–7 (How Animals Have Babies): children learn two big ideas — (1) different animals have young in different ways, some LAY EGGS (birds, and most fish, reptiles, amphibians and insects) and some give birth to LIVE YOUNG (most mammals); and (2) some babies look like miniature adults (lamb, chick, kitten) while others transform completely (tadpole→frog, caterpillar→butterfly) yet are still the SAME animal growing up. Teaching stays strictly on how babies ARRIVE (laid vs born) and GROW — not on reproduction mechanisms, which are developmentally later and RSE-governed. Activities combine an egg-layer vs live-bearer sort (with gentle surprises that break the mammal=live shortcut) and a 'grow the baby' metamorphosis sequence.
misconceptions: Believing ALL animals lay eggs, or that only birds/chickens lay eggs — missing that fish, reptiles, amphibians and insects lay eggs too.
Thinking every baby animal is just a smaller version of its parent — not expecting complete transformations like tadpole→frog or caterpillar→butterfly.
Assuming mammals never lay eggs and non-mammals never bear live young (the platypus and live-bearing sharks are real exceptions).
Thinking a caterpillar and its butterfly (or a tadpole and its frog) are different, unrelated animals rather than life stages of the SAME animal.
Conflating 'having babies' with human family framing; at this age it is simply 'laid as an egg or born live, then grows up'.

activities.title: Sort the animals: egg-layers or live-young?
steps: Place or group animal pictures into two bins: EGG-LAYERS and LIVE-YOUNG.
Put the hen, an egg-laying fish (e.g. a salmon or goldfish), frog, an egg-laying lizard (e.g. a gecko) and a beetle into the egg-layers bin; put the dog, cow, whale and human into the live-young bin.
After sorting with familiar animals, meet a surprise: a platypus (a mammal that LAYS eggs) and a shark that bears LIVE young — discuss why these are delightful exceptions, not new rules to memorise.
Say aloud one animal that lays eggs and one animal that has live babies.
activities.insight: Many kinds of animals lay eggs — not just birds — and most mammals have live young; nature also has surprising exceptions, so the shortcut 'mammals are born, everything else lays eggs' doesn't always hold.

activities.title: Grow the baby: watch a creature transform
steps: Advance a life-cycle sequence step by step: spawn → tadpole → froglet → frog, watching legs sprout and the tail shrink.
Advance a second sequence: egg → caterpillar → chrysalis → butterfly, watching the caterpillar eat, change into a chrysalis, and emerge as a butterfly.
After each transformation, decide and tag whether the grown-up 'looks the same' or 'looks different' from its baby.
Compare with a 'mini-adult' pairing: place a lamb beside a sheep and a chick beside a hen — these already look like small versions of their parents.
activities.insight: A tadpole IS a baby frog and a caterpillar IS a baby butterfly — the SAME animal at an early life stage. Some young change shape completely as they grow (metamorphosis) while others look like small versions of their parents from early on.

activities.title: Check and talk: same animal or different?
steps: Match each baby to its grown-up (baby→adult pairing).
Put life-stage cards in the right order (e.g. order the tadpole→frog stages).
Categorise a fresh set of animals as egg-layers or live-young.

Answer the diagnostic prompt: 'A frog lays eggs in a pond, and out come tadpoles that look nothing like frogs. Are the tadpoles baby frogs, or a completely different animal? How do you know — and what will happen to them as they grow?'
Discuss: Does a kitten look like a small cat or completely different? Do ALL babies look like their parents? What will grow on the tadpole, and what will disappear, as it gets bigger?
activities.insight: Children can give examples of egg-layers and live-bearers, and recognise that a very different-looking baby (tadpole, caterpillar) is still the same animal, which will change as it grows.

checkQuestion: A frog lays eggs in a pond, and out come tadpoles that look nothing like frogs. Are the tadpoles baby frogs, or a completely different animal? How do you know — and what will happen to them as they grow?
checkAnswer: The tadpoles ARE baby frogs — the same animal at an early stage of its life. As they grow they change (metamorphosis): they grow legs, lose the tail, and become frogs. They are not a different kind of animal and not fish.
